newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU finance ministers to tackle EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers to tackle EMU budget pact.

text.p: The difficult task of ensuring budgetary discipline among countries forming a common European currency is expected to top the agenda of a meeting of European Union finance ministers on Monday.

With the European Commission and the EU's monetary committee having worked hard to tackle the contentious and complex issue, the ministers will be asked to offer a road map on how to resolve several outstanding details.
"There are quite a number of technical and operational issues concerned," said one diplomat, adding that recent talks have focused on a "deepening of the process."

Enforcing budgetary rigour within economic and monetary union (EMU) is a prime concern for nearly all of the EU's 15 nations, but nowhere is the objective greater than in Germany, a country deeply wedded to sound monetary and budget policies.
Increasingly, German officials have become worried by what they perceive as a watering down of their initial proposal for the budget pact.

Coupled with growing political pressure to incorporate as many nations as possible in the first wave of EMU participants in 1999 and the sleight of hand accounting practices many have employed to try to qualify, German officials, led by Finance Minister Theo Waigel, are expected to toe a stringent line on budget discipline.
The target of their frustration will be the Commission's draft proposal for the stability pact, one that tries to reconcile differences over how tough such an accord should be.
One of the main areas of controversy is the lack of a precise definition of a severe economic downturn which would let governments running excessive deficits avoid sanctions.

Under the Commission's plan, a government found to have an annual deficit above three percent of total output would have to put forward a credible plan within a specified period -- 10 months -- to correct it.

If they failed, the offending country would have to make an initial deposit with the EU, worth 0.2 percent of GDP. For every percentage point above the three percent threshold, an added fine of 0.1 percent of GDP would be levied.

But if a country could demonstrate that its poor finances were due to an extraordinary economic downturn, it could presumably avoid any penalty. The Commission did not quantify the magnitude of a recession, but Germany very much wants to.

Earlier in the week EU monetary officials predicted that the complexity of such a debate would carry over into early next year, scuttling any chance of an agreement in time for the Dublin summit of EU leaders on December 13 and 14.
"What should come out of this meeting is the ministers saying do this or don't do that," said one EU official.
Such guidance would then form the basis for further talks by the EU's monetary committee, a group of national treasury and central banks officials.
Work between now and the end of November would then serve as a focal point for another ministerial meeting on December 2, the last one prior to the December summit.
